subsections.title: Bacterial Complexity and Nutrition
subsections.content_text: Though the bacterial structure is very simple, they are very complex in behaviour. Compared to many other organisms, bacteria as a group show the most extensive metabolic diversity. Some of the bacteria are autotrophic, i.e., they synthesise their own food from inorganic substrates. They may be photosynthetic autotrophic or chemosynthetic autotrophic. The vast majority of bacteria are heterotrophs, i.e., they depend on other organisms or on dead organic matter for food.

subsections.title: 2.1.1 Archaebacteria
subsections.content_text: These bacteria are special since they live in some of the most harsh habitats such as extreme salty areas (halophiles), hot springs (thermoacidophiles) and marshy areas (methanogens). Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure and this feature is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions. Methanogens are present in the gut of several ruminant animals such as cows and buffaloes and they are responsible for the production of methane (biogas) from the dung of these animals.

subsections.title: 2.1.2 Eubacteria
subsections.content_text: There are thousands of different eubacteria or ‘true bacteria’. They are characterised by the presence of a rigid cell wall, and if motile, a flagellum. The cyanobacteria (also referred to as blue-green algae) have chlorophyll $a$ similar to green plants and are photosynthetic autotrophs. The cyanobacteria are unicellular, colonial or filamentous, freshwater/marine or terrestrial algae. The colonies are generally surrounded by gelatinous sheath. They often form blooms in polluted water bodies. Some of these organisms can fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts, e.g., Nostoc and Anabaena. Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise various inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia and use the released energy for their ATP production. They play a great role in recycling nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorous, iron and sulphur.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.2
diagrams.description: A diagram of Nostoc, a filamentous blue-green algae. It shows a chain of cells (trichome) surrounded by a mucilaginous sheath. Specialized larger cells called heterocysts are visible within the filament, which are responsible for nitrogen fixation.

subsections.title: Heterotrophic Bacteria
subsections.content_text: Heterotrophic bacteria are most abundant in nature. The majority are important decomposers. Many of them have a significant impact on human affairs. They are helpful in making curd from milk, production of antibiotics, fixing nitrogen in legume roots, etc. Some are pathogens causing damage to human beings, crops, farm animals and pets. Cholera, typhoid, tetanus, citrus canker are well known diseases caused by different bacteria.

subsections.title: Bacterial Reproduction and Mycoplasma
subsections.content_text: Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission. Sometimes, under unfavourable conditions, they produce spores. They also reproduce by a sort of sexual reproduction by adopting a primitive type of DNA transfer from one bacterium to the other. The Mycoplasma are organisms that completely lack a cell wall. They are the smallest living cells known and can survive without oxygen. Many mycoplasma are pathogenic in animals and plants.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.3
diagrams.description: A diagram showing a bacterium undergoing binary fission. The cell wall and cell membrane are labeled, and the DNA is shown replicating and being distributed into two daughter cells as the cell constricts in the middle.

subsections.title: General Characteristics
subsections.content_text: All single-celled eukaryotes are placed under Protista, but the boundaries of this kingdom are not well defined. What may be ‘a photosynthetic protistan’ to one biologist may be ‘a plant’ to another. In this book we include Chrysophytes, Dinoflagellates, Euglenoids, Slime moulds and Protozoans under Protista. Members of Protista are primarily aquatic. This kingdom forms a link with the others dealing with plants, animals and fungi. Being eukaryotes, the protistan cell body contains a well defined nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. Some have flagella or cilia. Protists reproduce asexually and sexually by a process involving cell fusion and zygote formation.

subsections.title: 2.2.1 Chrysophytes
subsections.content_text: This group includes diatoms and golden algae (desmids). They are found in fresh water as well as in marine environments. They are microscopic and float passively in water currents (plankton). Most of them are photosynthetic. In diatoms the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells, which fit together as in a soap box. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible. Thus, diatoms have left behind large amount of cell wall deposits in their habitat; this accumulation over billions of years is referred to as ‘diatomaceous earth’. Being gritty this soil is used in polishing, filtration of oils and syrups. Diatoms are the chief ‘producers’ in the oceans.

subsections.title: 2.2.2 Dinoflagellates
subsections.content_text: These organisms are mostly marine and photosynthetic. They appear yellow, green, brown, blue or red depending on the main pigments present in their cells. The cell wall has stiff cellulose plates on the outer surface. Most of them have two flagella; one lies longitudinally and the other transversely in a furrow between the wall plates. Very often, red dinoflagellates (Example: Gonyaulax) undergo such rapid multiplication that they make the sea appear red (red tides). Toxins released by such large numbers may even kill other marine animals such as fishes.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.4
diagrams.description: A composite figure showing four types of protists: (a) a Dinoflagellate with its characteristic stiff cellulose plates and flagella; (b) Euglena, showing its spindle shape and flagellum; (c) a Slime mould appearing as a spreading plasmodial mass; (d) Paramoecium, a ciliated protozoan with its distinct slipper shape.

subsections.title: 2.2.3 Euglenoids
subsections.content_text: Majority of them are fresh water organisms found in stagnant water. Instead of a cell wall, they have a protein rich layer called pellicle which makes their body flexible. They have two flagella, a short and a long one. Though they are photosynthetic in the presence of sunlight, when deprived of sunlight they behave like heterotrophs by predating on other smaller organisms. Interestingly, the pigments of euglenoids are identical to those present in higher plants. Example: Euglena.

subsections.title: 2.2.4 Slime Moulds
subsections.content_text: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists. The body moves along decaying twigs and leaves engulfing organic material. Under suitable conditions, they form an aggregation called plasmodium which may grow and spread over several feet. During unfavourable conditions, the plasmodium differentiates and forms fruiting bodies bearing spores at their tips. The spores possess true walls. They are extremely resistant and survive for many years, even under adverse conditions. The spores are dispersed by air currents.

subsections.title: 2.2.5 Protozoans
subsections.content_text: All protozoans are heterotrophs and live as predators or parasites. They are believed to be primitive relatives of animals. There are four major groups of protozoans. Amoeboid protozoans: These organisms live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil. They move and capture Amoeboid protozoans live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil. They move and capture their prey by putting out pseudopodia (false feet) as in Amoeba. Marine forms have silica shells on their surface. Some of them such as Entamoeba are parasites.

subsections.title: Flagellated Protozoans
subsections.content_text: The members of this group are either free-living or parasitic. They have flagella. The parasitic forms cause diseases such as sleeping sickness. Example: Trypanosoma.

subsections.title: Ciliated Protozoans
subsections.content_text: These are aquatic, actively moving organisms because of the presence of thousands of cilia. They have a cavity (gullet) that opens to the outside of the cell surface. The coordinated movement of rows of cilia causes the water laden with food to be steered into the gullet. Example: Paramoecium.

subsections.title: Sporozoans
subsections.content_text: This includes diverse organisms that have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle. The most notorious is Plasmodium (malarial parasite) which causes malaria, a disease which has a staggering effect on human population.

subsections.title: General Characteristics and Habitat
subsections.content_text: The fungi constitute a unique kingdom of heterotrophic organisms. They show a great diversity in morphology and habitat. Common examples include fungi on moist bread, rotten fruits, mushrooms, and toadstools. White spots seen on mustard leaves are due to a parasitic fungus. Some fungi are unicellular, such as yeast (used to make bread and beer), while others cause diseases in plants and animals, like the wheat rust-causing Puccinia. Some are sources of antibiotics, such as Penicillium. Fungi are cosmopolitan and occur in air, water, soil, and on animals and plants. They prefer to grow in warm and humid places.

subsections.title: Morphology and Cellular Structure
subsections.content_text: With the exception of yeasts which are unicellular, fungi are filamentous. Their bodies consist of long, slender thread-like structures called hyphae. The network of hyphae is known as mycelium. Some hyphae are continuous tubes filled with multinucleated cytoplasm; these are called coenocytic hyphae. Others have septae or cross walls in their hyphae. The cell walls of fungi are composed of chitin and polysaccharides.

subsections.title: Modes of Nutrition
subsections.content_text: Most fungi are heterotrophic and absorb soluble organic matter from dead substrates and hence are called saprophytes. Those that depend on living plants and animals are called parasites. They can also live as symbionts—in association with algae as lichens and with roots of higher plants as mycorrhiza.

subsections.title: Reproduction and Spore Types
subsections.content_text: Reproduction in fungi can take place by vegetative means—fragmentation, fission and budding. Asexual reproduction is by spores called conidia or sporangiospores or zoospores, and sexual reproduction is by oospores, ascospores and basidiospores. The various spores are produced in distinct structures called fruiting bodies.

subsections.title: The Sexual Cycle and Dikaryophase
subsections.content_text: The sexual cycle involves the following three steps: (i) Fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes called plasmogamy. (ii) Fusion of two nuclei called karyogamy. (iii) Meiosis in zygote resulting in haploid spores. When a fungus reproduces sexually, two haploid hyphae of compatible mating types come together and fuse. In some fungi, the fusion of two haploid cells immediately results in diploid cells ($2n$). However, in other fungi (ascomycetes and basidiomycetes), an intervening dikaryotic stage ($n + n$, i.e., two nuclei per cell) occurs; such a condition is called a dikaryon and the phase is called dikaryophase of fungus. Later, the parental nuclei fuse and the cells become diploid. Fungi form fruiting bodies in which reduction division occurs, leading to formation of haploid spores.

subsections.title: Basis of Classification
subsections.content_text: The morphology of the mycelium, mode of spore formation and fruiting bodies form the basis for the division of the kingdom into various classes.

subsections.title: 2.3.1 Phycomycetes
subsections.content_text: Members of phycomycetes are found in aquatic habitats and on decaying wood in moist and damp places or as obligate parasites on plants. The mycelium is aseptate and coenocytic. Asexual reproduction takes place by zoospores (motile) or by aplanospores (non-motile). These spores are endogenously produced in sporangium. A zygospore is formed by fusion of two gametes. These gametes are similar in morphology (isogamous) or dissimilar (anisogamous or oogamous). Some common examples are Mucor, Rhizopus (the bread mould) and Albugo (the parasitic fungi on mustard).

diagrams.label: Figure 2.5 (a)
diagrams.description: Microscopic view of Mucor showing sporangia and hyphae.

subsections.title: 2.3.2 Ascomycetes
subsections.content_text: Commonly known as sac-fungi, the ascomycetes are mostly multicellular, e.g., Penicillium, or rarely unicellular, e.g., yeast (Saccharomyces). They are saprophytic, decomposers, parasitic or coprophilous (growing on dung). Mycelium is branched and septate. The asexual spores are conidia produced exogenously on the special mycelium called conidiophores. Conidia on germination produce mycelium. Sexual spores are called ascospores which are produced endogenously in sac like asci (singular ascus). These asci are arranged in different types of fruiting bodies called ascocarps. Some examples are Aspergillus, Claviceps and Neurospora. Neurospora is used extensively in biochemical and genetic work. Many members like morels and truffles are edible and are considered delicacies.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.5 (b)
diagrams.description: Microscopic view of Aspergillus showing conidiophores and conidia.

subsections.title: 2.3.3 Basidiomycetes
subsections.content_text: Commonly known forms of basidiomycetes are mushrooms, bracket fungi or puffballs. They grow in soil, on logs and tree stumps and in living plant bodies as parasites, e.g., rusts and smuts. The mycelium is branched and septate. The asexual spores are generally not found, but vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common. The sex organs are absent, but plasmogamy is brought about by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains or genotypes. The resultant structure is dikaryotic which ultimately gives rise to basidium. Karyogamy and meiosis take place in the basidium producing four basidiospores. The basidiospores are exogenously produced on the basidium (pl.: basidia). The basidia are arranged in fruiting bodies called basidiocarps. Some common members are Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut) and Puccinia (rust fungus).

diagrams.label: Figure 2.5 (c)
diagrams.description: Illustration of Agaricus, a common mushroom.

subsections.title: 2.3.4 Deuteromycetes
subsections.content_text: Commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known. When the sexual forms of these fungi were discovered they were moved into classes they rightly belong to. It is also possible that the asexual and vegetative stage have been given one name (and placed under deuteromycetes) and the sexual stage another (and placed under another class). Later when the linkages were established, the fungi were correctly identified and moved out of deuteromycetes. Once perfect (sexual) stages of members of deuteromycetes were discovered, they were often moved to ascomycetes and basidiomycetes. The deuteromycetes reproduce only by asexual spores known as conidia. The mycelium is septate and branched. Some members are saprophytes or parasites while a large number of them are decomposers of litter and help in mineral cycling. Some examples are Alternaria, Colletotrichum and Trichoderma.

subsections.title: Characteristics of Kingdom Plantae
subsections.content_text: Kingdom Plantae includes all eukaryotic chlorophyll-containing organisms commonly called plants. While most are autotrophic, a few members are partially heterotrophic, such as insectivorous plants (e.g., Bladderwort and Venus fly trap) or parasites (e.g., Cuscuta). Plant cells possess an eukaryotic structure with prominent chloroplasts and a cell wall primarily composed of cellulose. This kingdom encompasses diverse groups including algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms. Detailed study of eukaryotic cell structure is covered in Chapter 8.

subsections.title: Alternation of Generations
subsections.content_text: The life cycle of plants is characterized by two distinct phases: the diploid sporophytic phase and the haploid gametophytic phase. These phases alternate with each other in a phenomenon known as alternation of generations. The relative lengths of these haploid and diploid phases, and whether they are free-living or dependent on others, vary significantly among different plant groups. Further details of this kingdom are explored in Chapter 3.

subsections.title: Characteristics of Kingdom Animalia
subsections.content_text: Kingdom Animalia is characterized by heterotrophic eukaryotic organisms that are multicellular and lack cell walls. They depend directly or indirectly on plants for food. Animals digest their food in an internal cavity and store food reserves in the form of glycogen or fat. Their mode of nutrition is holozoic, involving the ingestion of food. They follow a definite growth pattern, developing into adults with a specific shape and size. Higher forms exhibit elaborate sensory and neuromotor mechanisms. Most animals are capable of locomotion. Sexual reproduction typically involves the copulation of male and female, followed by embryological development. Salient features of various phyla are described in Chapter 4.

subsections.title: General Nature of Viruses
subsections.content_text: In Whittaker's five-kingdom classification, there is no mention of lichens or acellular organisms like viruses, viroids, and prions. Viruses are not considered truly 'living' because they do not possess a cell structure. Instead, they are non-cellular organisms characterized by an inert crystalline structure outside a living cell. Once they infect a host cell, they take over its machinery to replicate themselves, often killing the host. Consequently, viruses are classified as obligate parasites.

subsections.title: Historical Milestones in Virology
subsections.content_text: The name 'virus' means venom or poisonous fluid. Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892) identified certain microbes as the causal agents of the mosaic disease of tobacco; these were found to be smaller than bacteria as they passed through bacteria-proof filters. M.W. Beijerinck (1898) demonstrated that the extract of infected tobacco plants could cause infection in healthy plants, naming the fluid *Contagium vivum fluidum* (infectious living fluid). W.M. Stanley (1935) showed that viruses could be crystallized, with the crystals consisting largely of proteins.

subsections.title: Viral Structure and Composition
subsections.content_text: In addition to proteins, viruses contain genetic material, which can be either RNA or DNA, but never both. A virus is essentially a nucleoprotein, and its genetic material is the infectious component. Generally, viruses that infect plants have single-stranded RNA, while those that infect animals have either single or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA. Bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect bacteria, are usually double-stranded DNA viruses. The nucleic acid is protected by a protein coat called the capsid, which is composed of small subunits called capsomeres. These capsomeres are arranged in helical or polyhedral geometric forms.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.6 (a)
diagrams.description: Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) showing a rod-shaped structure with a helical arrangement of capsomeres forming the capsid and an internal RNA strand.

diagrams.label: Figure 2.6 (b)
diagrams.description: A Bacteriophage showing a complex structure with a polyhedral head, a collar, a sheath, and tail fibers.

subsections.title: Viral Pathogenesis and Symptoms
subsections.content_text: Viruses are responsible for various diseases. In humans, they cause mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, and AIDS. In plants, viral symptoms include mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing, and stunted growth.

subsections.title: Viroids
subsections.content_text: Viroids were discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971 as a new infectious agent smaller than viruses. They cause potato spindle tuber disease. A viroid consists of free RNA and lacks the protein coat found in viruses. The RNA of the viroid is of low molecular weight.

subsections.title: Prions
subsections.content_text: Prions are agents consisting of abnormally folded proteins that cause certain infectious neurological diseases. They are similar in size to viruses. Notable diseases caused by prions include bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly known as mad cow disease in cattle, and its human variant, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

subsections.title: Lichens
subsections.content_text: Lichens are symbiotic associations, representing mutually useful relationships between algae and fungi. The algal component is known as the phycobiont (autotrophic), and the fungal component is the mycobiont (heterotrophic). Algae prepare food for fungi, while fungi provide shelter and absorb mineral nutrients and water for their partner. Lichens are highly sensitive to pollution and serve as excellent pollution indicators, as they do not grow in polluted areas.

subsections.title: Chapter Overview
subsections.content_text: Biological classification was first proposed by Aristotle based on simple morphological characters. Linnaeus later classified organisms into two kingdoms – Plantae and Animalia. Whittaker proposed an elaborate five kingdom classification – Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, based on criteria like cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships. In this system, bacteria are in Monera, single-celled eukaryotes in Protista, and diverse saprophytic organisms in Fungi. items.problem: Discuss how classification systems have undergone several changes over a period of time?
items.solution: Classification systems have evolved from simple morphological groupings to complex systems based on multiple criteria. Initially, Linnaeus proposed a Two Kingdom system (Plantae and Animalia). This was found inadequate as it didn't distinguish between eukaryotes and prokaryotes, unicellular and multicellular organisms, or photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic organisms. R.H. Whittaker later proposed the Five Kingdom classification (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia) based on cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships. Recently, a three-domain system has also been proposed to further divide Kingdom Monera.

items.problem: State two economically important uses of: (a) heterotrophic bacteria (b) archaebacteria
items.solution: (a) Heterotrophic bacteria: 1. They are used in the production of curd from milk (Lactobacillus). 2. They are used in the production of antibiotics and fixing nitrogen in legume roots. (b) Archaebacteria: 1. Methanogens are used in the production of methane (biogas) from the dung of ruminant animals. 2. They are studied for their ability to survive in extreme environments, which has applications in biotechnology.

items.problem: What is the nature of cell-walls in diatoms?
items.solution: In diatoms, the cell walls form two thin overlapping shells which fit together as in a soap box. The walls are embedded with silica and thus the walls are indestructible. This leaves behind large amounts of cell wall deposits in their habitat, referred to as 'diatomaceous earth'.

items.problem: Find out what do the terms ‘algal bloom’ and ‘red-tides’ signify.
items.solution: ‘Algal bloom’ refers to the rapid increase or accumulation in the population of algae (typically cyanobacteria) in freshwater or marine water systems, often resulting in a change of color and depletion of oxygen. ‘Red-tides’ are caused by the rapid multiplication of red dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax, which make the sea appear red and can release toxins that kill other marine animals.

items.problem: How are viroids different from viruses?
items.solution: Viroids differ from viruses in the following ways: 1. Viroids are smaller in size. 2. They lack the protein coat (capsid) that is present in viruses. 3. The genetic material in viroids is free RNA of low molecular weight, whereas viruses have either DNA or RNA enclosed in a protein coat.

items.problem: Describe briefly the four major groups of Protozoa.
items.solution: The four major groups of Protozoa are: 1. Amoeboid protozoans: Live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil; move and capture prey by putting out pseudopodia (e.g., Amoeba). 2. Flagellated protozoans: Either free-living or parasitic; have flagella (e.g., Trypanosoma). 3. Ciliated protozoans: Aquatic, actively moving organisms because of the presence of thousands of cilia (e.g., Paramoecium). 4. Sporozoans: Include diverse organisms that have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle (e.g., Plasmodium).

items.problem: Plants are autotrophic. Can you think of some plants that are partially heterotrophic?
items.solution: Yes, some plants are partially heterotrophic. These include: 1. Insectivorous plants like Venus flytrap and bladderwort, which trap insects to supplement their nitrogen requirements. 2. Parasitic plants like Cuscuta (Amarbel), which lack chlorophyll and derive nutrition from a host plant.

items.problem: What do the terms phycobiont and mycobiont signify?
items.solution: In a lichen, which is a symbiotic association between algae and fungi, the algal component is known as the phycobiont and the fungal component is known as the mycobiont. The phycobiont is autotrophic and prepares food for the fungus, while the mycobiont is heterotrophic and provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water for its partner.

items.problem: Give a comparative account of the classes of Kingdom Fungi under the following: (i) mode of nutrition (ii) mode of reproduction
items.solution: (i) Mode of Nutrition: Phycomycetes are obligate parasites on plants or saprophytic on decaying wood. Ascomycetes are saprophytic, decomposers, parasitic or coprophilous (growing on dung). Basidiomycetes grow in soil, on logs and tree stumps and in living plant bodies as parasites (rusts and smuts). Deuteromycetes are primarily decomposers of litter. (ii) Mode of Reproduction: Phycomycetes reproduce asexually by zoospores or aplanospores and sexually by zygospores. Ascomycetes reproduce asexually by conidia and sexually by ascospores produced in asci. Basidiomycetes lack asexual spores; sexual reproduction occurs by plasmogamy of vegetative cells to form a dikaryotic mycelium which gives rise to basidiospores. Deuteromycetes only reproduce by asexual spores (conidia); their sexual stage is unknown.

items.problem: What are the characteristic features of Euglenoids?
items.solution: Characteristic features of Euglenoids include: 1. They are fresh water organisms found in stagnant water. 2. Instead of a cell wall, they have a protein-rich layer called pellicle which makes their body flexible. 3. They have two flagella, a short and a long one. 4. They are photosynthetic in the presence of sunlight, but behave like heterotrophs by predating on other smaller organisms when deprived of sunlight.

items.problem: Give a brief account of viruses with respect to their structure and nature of genetic material. Also name four common viral diseases.
items.solution: Structure: Viruses are non-cellular organisms characterized by having an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell. They consist of a protein coat called a capsid made of small subunits called capsomeres, which protects the nucleic acid. Genetic Material: Viruses contain either DNA or RNA, never both. Generally, plant viruses have single-stranded RNA, animal viruses have either single or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA, and bacteriophages have double-stranded DNA. Common viral diseases: Mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, and AIDS.

items.problem: Organise a discussion in your class on the topic – Are viruses living or non-living?
items.solution: Viruses occupy a twilight zone between living and non-living. Arguments for non-living: They are inert crystalline structures outside a host, they cannot reproduce on their own, and they lack cellular machinery. Arguments for living: They contain genetic material (DNA or RNA), they can replicate and multiply once they infect a host cell, and they can undergo mutations. Therefore, they are often described as 'obligate parasites' or 'biological entities' at the edge of life.
